requests.text: E1 has an independently supportable possessory ground for injunctive restraint against E2's interference with settled possession of E3, notwithstanding E1's failure to establish proprietary title. This conclusion depends on S3, which depends on S2's accepted judicial settled-possession classification and S1's preservation of possession despite title non-proof. It supports protection against interference without determining every independent requirement for injunctive relief or confirming ownership.

requests.text: Because possession-based protection does not determine ownership, the Supreme Court expressly reserved title, and E2 had not established the title needed to justify eviction in the reviewed proceedings, the parties may pursue competing proprietary claims in duly constituted proceedings. E2's prospective title-based eviction depends on establishing a better right to possession. The conclusion does not establish any present right of self-help eviction or predict the result of future litigation.

counterarguments: The appellant contended that omitting a declaration of title rendered the suit defective; the Supreme Court rejected automatic dismissal in this merits-stage case (IK-789051:L68-L69; L109-L112).

The appellant separately argued that plaintiff title non-proof required dismissal irrespective of established possession or defendant title; the Court found no merit in this submission (IK-789051:L69).

Sri Dasnam Naga Sanyasi was invoked against an injunction-only suit, but the Supreme Court described it as a discretionary temporary-injunction decision on its own facts, not a merits-stage automatic bar (IK-789051:L108-L110).

Settled possession is necessary: stray, intermittent, incipient or incomplete trespass can be resisted with no more force than permitted; the duration, knowledge, acquiescence and possessory-intention factors are not independently proved here (IK-789051:L88-L105).

Even a rightful owner may need judicial process against settled possession, while a wrongfully dispossessed rightful owner may retake land peacefully and a claimant proving better right may seek judicial eviction; the protective rule is not immunity from lawful recovery (IK-789051:L85-L87; L107).

Neither side proved title sufficient for its proposed consequence, and the apparent boundary dispute remains unresolved; possession-based injunction and dismissed appeal do not settle either ownership or demarcation (IK-789051:L65-L67; L106-L107; L113-L114).

all_raw_relations.reason: The Trial Court's affirmative possession finding supplies the established-possession component of the independent possessory basis.

The separate title non-proof finding establishes the circumstance in which the Court nonetheless preserved the plaintiff's possession-based ground; it is not treated as affirmative evidence of possession.

The plaintiff alleged title, but the subsequent judicial finding records failure to prove it. The allegation does not establish ownership, and failure of proof does not conclusively disprove the alleged ownership.
The independent possessory basis permits evaluation of protection for settled possession without first establishing proprietary title.
The express judicial settled-possession finding supplies the case-specific classification required for the protective rule, subject to its open-text limitations.
The absence of a merely transient classification follows from the judicial classification of possession as settled. It is not independent negative evidence about the chronology of occupation.
Legally protectable settled possession supplies the protected interest required for possession-based injunctive restraint.
The defendant's reported obstruction of construction supplies the relevant attempted interference with the plaintiff's established possession.

The defendant's accompanying ownership assertion identifies the competing claim invoked during the interference. The relation supports the characterization of the episode, not the truth of defendant ownership.

The defendant asserted ownership but failed to establish title sufficient to justify eviction. These propositions are not logically contradictory because non-proof does not establish absence of ownership.
Counsel advanced the contrary position that omission of declaratory relief rendered the suit defective. The relation records opposition by argument, not a judicially accepted defect.
Counsel separately argued that title non-proof required dismissal even if possession was established. The Supreme Court rejected this proposed automatic consequence.
The independently supportable possessory ground explains why the appellant's title-based objections do not automatically require dismissal.
The target court's distinction between merits adjudication and discretionary interim relief limits the force of the appellant's reliance on the Allahabad decision.
Because the identified basis of relief is settled possession and interference, it does not itself entail proprietary ownership or determine the competing title.
The Trial Court's reported decision to leave title open confirms the limited possessory scope of the lower adjudication.
The reported High Court reservation reinforces that the protection of possession did not settle the proprietary dispute.
The Supreme Court's explicit clarification directly supports the conclusion that possessory relief does not constitute title confirmation for either party.
The non-determination of title explains why a separate proprietary adjudication remains available.
The express judicial reservation establishes that the parties may seek determination of their claimed titles in duly constituted proceedings.
The defendant's failure to establish the title necessary to justify eviction explains why any future title-based recovery remains conditional on proof of a better right to possess.

The unresolved boundary demarcation limits what can presently be concluded about any future proprietary proceeding. Availability of that proceeding does not establish the land boundaries or competing rights.
The possession-based ground forms part of the reasoning supporting the appellate outcome. The direction is from reasoning to disposition, never from disposition to antecedent proof.
Rejection of the appellant's proposed automatic title-based dismissal grounds contributes to the stated disposition without using that disposition to validate the legal or factual premises.
